title: What is Zen, Part 2
speaker: Shuko Edie Norton and Shin-yu Scott Allen
summary: The main teaching of this Soto Zen dharma talk emphasizes the importance of having guidance in one's spiritual practice, particularly when it comes to navigating complex questions and doubts. The speaker shares their personal experiences with multiple teachers who have helped them deepen their understanding of Buddhist teachings such as emptiness and perception. By working with a teacher or exploring different perspectives, individuals can cultivate mindfulness, wisdom, and compassion, ultimately leading to a more authentic and fulfilling Zen practice.

**Shuko Edie Norton:** A Dharma seminar for July, which is about the book *What is Zen* that Norman Fischer and Susan Moon wrote and published together.
So this evening's topic is teachers.
I'm going to start, and then Scott is going to finish.
So that's done.
Okay, thank you.
There are questions in this book.
Susan asked the questions, and some of them are elaborate and some of them are simple.
Then Norman answers in a really clear, clarifying way.
I highly recommend the book, whether you're new or old, long term or short term.
It's a lovely book.
So I'm going to answer some of the early questions in that chapter.
The first one is: do you have to have a teacher?
Norman says no, you don't.
Zazen is a practice in and of itself that anyone can do.
It's a practice in its own right, and you learn a lot from doing it.
However, if you can find a teacher and work with a teacher, you will benefit greatly.
It will help you interpret your experience, it will help you learn Buddhist teachings and Zen teachings, and you will grow as a person.

The Sangha and the teachers are really integral and interrelated, and in a way you can't have a really full Zen experience without teachers, including all of us, members as well as designated teachers.
I'm going to tell you a little bit about my first teachers.
My first one was straight out of Japan, back in the 70s.
He was invited by Suzuki Roshi, who was the head of the San Francisco Zen Center starting in the late 60s.

Suzuki Roshi invited Kobun, who lived in Japan and was part of a temple family, to come over and help set up Tassajara, which the San Francisco Zen Center had recently purchased and set up as a monastery.
The first Japanese monastery in the U.S., and I guess the only one on the west coast still.
Kobun then became a teacher at Haiku Zendo, which was in Los Altos, California, about 40 miles south of San Francisco.
Suzuki Roshi had a student who lived in Los Altos who invited him to come down maybe every week or every two weeks or so to give a talk there, and he gathered some students.
So when Kobun moved into that neighborhood, he and his family, he became the teacher for the Haiku Zendo group, which was flourishing at that point.
I met Kobun probably two years after he was first in the U.S. and became that teacher.
I had been reading about Zen and found it perplexing and fascinating.
I began to sense Zen based on that book, *The Three Pillars of Zen*, which had illustrations in the back about how you sit down, which is just totally bizarre.
It's like trying to learn yoga through illustrations.
I did it for a while and I thought, I'm sure I'm not doing this right, and I wish I could talk with somebody about it.
And just then, like the next week, in the newspaper there was an ad saying that this Japanese teacher was going to come to Foothill College and teach a class for a full quarter on Zen.
So I thought, this is my chance.
I signed up, and I was really scared to go because I thought it was very unusual.
It was not at all what my background had been, but I really wanted to learn about it.
I expected there might be 10 or 12 students there.
When I got there, there were like 80 students in this room, there were nearly enough chairs, and a lot of us were sitting on the floor.
We waited and waited and waited, for about 20 minutes after the class started.
Finally Kobun, who was maybe in his mid-30s at that time, kind of floated in with this beautiful black gown and precise collar, very unlike mine, and a bald shiny head and a big smile on his face.
He was just like some kind of visitation.
It was really wonderful.
He spoke English pretty well, but he had a very thick Japanese accent, so I didn't get much of what he said.
But he was just so inspiring in his being that he seemed like a wonderful, wonderful person.
Toward the end of this 10-week course, he invited some of us, anybody who wanted to, to come to the Haiku Zendo on Wednesday evenings.
They had Wednesday evenings in those days too, like we do now.
A few of us went, and the zendo was in a two-car garage in the home of this woman who had initially invited Suzuki Roshi to talk there.
They had converted it into a beautiful zendo.
It was just spectacular, so exotic and full of incense and candlelight and beautiful zabutons and zafus and tatami mats and all that.
It was like, I don't know, a dream.
I was immediately captivated by the whole thing, and never, never, ever missed a single night after that.
I joined the group, the sangha.
I became a regular student, went to classes, went to a lot of things there, and tried to understand what Zen was about.
There was a thing where you could have dokusan with the teacher, and I didn't know what that was about or what you were supposed to say.
I had been a pretty academic person, so I took a lot of my books there and said, okay, now I want you to explain this and I want you to explain this, and that kind of stuff.
He was very patient with me.
I kept asking about emptiness: what's this emptiness?
What does that mean?
He would say something that I didn't understand, of course, so I would ask him again and again.
Finally he gave me this book of [unclear: "Narachuna"].
It's the third century scholar on Buddhism explaining emptiness, and it was called emptiness.
Of course, it was totally indecipherable for me.
And I thought, well, that was really a joke.
That was his answer.
You can't explain emptiness.
Or if you could explain it, nobody could understand what it was.
So Kobun was a lovely, lovely person.
We have a picture here in our ancestors thing in the library.
This is Kobun as a bit older person than he was when he first arrived.
You might look at that.
There's a wonderful book put out by one of his students in more recent years that gives lots of pictures of him and lots of sayings of his.
He was particularly kind and receptive to people and just said, you're fine just as you are.
I really appreciated that, because in those days I wasn't feeling that I was at all fine.
Let's read something that's like that.
He said:
*Listen to the truth.
If there's any misunderstandings about what is called Zen life or Buddhist life, I'd like to clear them up and reassure you that however you are is the way you should be.
Sweet.
And [unclear: "Buddha's enlightenment and humankind has a topic"].
When we are in the muddy road, to hate being in the muddy road doesn't do anything.
The first thing is to step out of it or to find how to walk in the muddy road.
Hatred is extra.
If there is some problem, kindly deal with it and take care of it yourself in the right way.*
So he was able to work with students where the student was.
Even though I didn't know quite how to handle going to him for dokusan, a few years later he was still my teacher.
I had a big crisis in my family.
My husband was going to die, and I knew that.
I called Kobun and said, what should I do?
Kobun helped me with that very directly, in a very practical way.
When my husband did die, he was a suicide.
Kobun was right there, came immediately to my house, and did a ceremony for me and did other following ceremonies.
He was just a person who accepted where everyone was and supported us wherever we needed that support.
So he was a wonderful teacher.
About five years into my being part of Haiku Zendo and his student, I did ask for jukai and was given a rakusu and took the precepts and so forth.
But sometime after that, he decided that he didn't want to teach there anymore.
He didn't want to be the head of a sangha.
He wanted to be a traveling teacher, and had all over the world places to go and teach and so forth.
Well, everyone was shocked.
I didn't know what to think of that.
I myself thought you had to have a teacher for life.
You know, that was it.
You got only one chance and then they couldn't go away.
It was kind of the [unclear: "Guro"] time where you followed forever.
It turns out that Zen doesn't require that, fortunately.
But some people wouldn't let him go.
They just moved with him to where he went, to New Mexico, Santa Cruz, California, wherever it was, and I suppose supported him in some way.
But I thought he had been so helpful to me, and he truly wanted to escape from us, to not do that type of leadership anymore.
So with a lot of pain, I gave him up, allowed him to leave us, and didn't see him more than a couple of times after that, every long time.
He was always very warmly happy to see me when that happened.
So it was a true love relationship with this teacher.
It was wonderful to have that early in my Zen life.
I was without that kind of contact and connection for a good ten years.
And then I met and began to sit with Reb Anderson.
I do also have a picture of him at San Francisco Zen Center.
He was and has been [unclear: "an avid"] at the San Francisco Zen Center, and a very fine teacher, very bright, a brilliant guy, very analytical, very unconventionally, not so social.
Maybe didn't know all of it, but very refined and so forth.
He was an amazing teacher for me because during the years that I was studying with Kobun and couldn't understand some of the things that he said, I missed a lot of teachings, I think.
And Reb had a lot of insight into the Buddhist teachings about emptiness, for one thing.
No self, how perception happens, karma, things like that, that are really abstruse and difficult for Westerners to understand.
So I learned a great deal from him.
The final thing that I did with him was in 2000: I went to a winter three-week practice period at Green Gulch Monastery, which is part of the San Francisco group.
I had forgotten to take my rakusu that Kobun had given me many years before.
I was really crushed that I had forgotten.
This thing is so precious to me.
And then I finally thought, well, maybe it's time for me to let him go entirely.
It was maybe 20 years or something since I'd been close with him.
So I talked to Reb about it and asked him if he would be willing to give me the precepts again.
I'd already arranged for him to be my teacher and he had accepted that.
He did do that.
I made my first rakusu.
Kobun had given me one from Japan, but I made one for myself, and that was a lovely experience.
Then Reb was my teacher for the next probably six years, seven years, something like that, and I got a lot from him.
He not only taught at Green Gulch, but he was no longer Abbot, so he could teach more widely, and he did retreats at various other centers.
I was able to practice with him and learn so much from him.
Then I came here, 15, going on 16 years ago, moved up here.
Tim joined the practice group that we were developing and took over time.
Tim was the main guy, the head guy then, and grew and grew and became not only ordained but transmitted as a teacher.
Now he's our, what do we call him?
A guiding teacher and so forth.
He was kind enough to ordain me as a priest five years ago in 2013.
So the second question that I wanted to answer from the book was: can you have more than one teacher?
Well, yeah, I did.
I found out that I could, and I was really happy that I had those opportunities.
I lived in an area in California until 2003 when I came here, which was just loaded with all kinds of Buddhist teachers.
So I had lots of opportunities to study with many different teachers.
Jack Kornfield, you've probably heard of.
I studied with him quite a bit.
And with Norman when he was at Green Gulch as a priest, with somebody called Gil [unclear: "Kronzdale"] who's written a number of things.
He's both a Zen teacher and a Vipassana teacher.
Yvonne Rand, who was his old Zen teacher from the original group of people, then learned a lot of Tibetan practices, and I studied with her for a certain amount of time.
I was able to go and sit with Thich Nhat Hanh at two different large group meetings and hear him speak.
I joined and practiced with various Tibetan groups and Vipassana groups.
So it was kind of a smorgasbord that was going on in the Bay Area and everything.
It's good to experience numerous other teachers.
And we actually have a fair number of really good teachers within our reach.
We have Kate and Michael up in British Columbia, who are fine teachers.
I think they're open for practice on Sundays, and you could go up there.
Seattle Soto Zen, we can go down and visit with them and sit with them, also I think on Sundays.
The Olympia Zen Center has a lovely zendo and a regular practice that we can take part in.
Anita Feng is a Korean Zen practice in the northern part of Seattle.
The VIMS group here that we share the building with frequently has good teachers coming for weekends or even for just one evening's talk, and we can take advantage of that.
And of course we can, and people have, gone to other zendo centers in Oregon and in California.
So if you want to, you can do it.
But also teachers, our sangha members, just us, who bump around against each other, like getting a rock polisher.
That's the metaphor for what the sangha life is.
It wears down our sharp edges and polishes us up, and sometimes it's uncomfortable,
but we live through it and we're grateful for it.
So sangha members are also our regular teachers daily, and we practice silently together, which teaches us a lot.
We work as volunteers together, which teaches us even more, because sometimes we don't work in the same ways and struggle together.
We benefit from the wisdom and talent of each other as Dharma friends.
So we're not social friends.
My experience with sangha members is that we're not social friends so much as we're essential spiritual friends, and that's a very special relationship.

We also have a mentoring program here where newer people can request mentoring, which is meeting with a more senior person periodically for a period of six months or a year and talking about what the student wants.
We have lots of Dharma talks and dokusan and practice discussions and shuso classes when we have a shuso head student.
So we do have lots of ways of teaching each other.
Third and last: what is meant by Zen training?
Sometimes you hear, I'm training as a Zen student.
In a way, it's kind of boot camp.
If you're in a sesshin, it feels like a big rigorous effort.

But zazen is training the mind and body, watching the mind carefully, observing what it's doing, and training the body to move in specific, very finely tuned ways, working with the breath, working with posture, working with movement.
Buddhist teachings train us how to conceive and think about reality from a certain perspective.
A teacher can be like a coach or a music teacher.
You're both devoted to the practice, and the teacher guides you, the student, toward better and better expression.

Learning all of Zen's forms is a kind of training: how to hold the hands, how to sit correctly, how to sit quietly, how to move in the zendo, how to bow, how to work with the altar, all the different roles, very specific things that you learn.
Those are trainings.
Zazen and the forms instill discipline.
They want us to be exact here, now, paying attention.
Reb once said that he could tell when people are trying too hard by looking at how they move in the zendo.

They're kind of exaggerating their erectness or something, or if they're not quite sure they really should be doing this, they're kind of doubtful and maybe resist and they kind of slide in here and do that.
So he said a lot can be seen in the physical behavior of people, as to where they are, and he encouraged everyone to be just right there,
*[Shuko Edie Norton and Shin-yu Scott Allen share this talk.

doing it enough, but not too much, that kind of thing.
That's being in the present, which is the big teaching.
That's what I want to say.
Can you keep time for me?
Okay.
Maybe.
Well, that one makes too much noise.
Okay, you have a good half hour.
**Shin-yu Scott Allen:** The first question I wanted to address was, do you have to have a teacher in order to practice Zen?
And Norm says it depends on your intentions, goals and circumstances.
I'm lucky enough to talk with a lot of newcomers, and when I ask them why they're here, about nine times out of ten they'll say something like, "Well, I read a couple of books on the subject.
It sounds interesting.
And I've meditated a couple of times."
I'm a very recent graduate.
And that was my story too.
In my travels through Asia, I saw thousands and thousands of people who didn't have too much material wealth.
They were living in little shacks along the river, generally.
But they seemed so happy.
And about every block, there's another Buddhist temple or shrine.
I said, "Well, maybe there's something to this Buddhism thing."
So I did the same thing: read a few books, started meditating.
I didn't even think about a teacher.
It wasn't even in my brain scan at that point.
That seems kind of primitive now, but I remember reading a story about [unclear: "John Day of Laura"].
He's a recently deceased abbot of the Mountain and Rivers Order in New York, and he started out the same way.
He read a few books and he meditated.
He was working at a job, and the only quiet place he could find was a closet.
So he would meditate during his lunch break, sitting in a closet.
And then it grew from there.
I fully believe that old saying, when you're ready, a teacher will appear.
And it did for me.
I got the feeling that I needed to practice with other people.
I was thinking more in terms of a car club or something like that.
I wasn't thinking about a Zen center.
But I knew I just wanted to be with other people who shared my interests.
And not too long thereafter, I was lucky enough to see an ad in the newspaper.
The ad said, "Change your mind today."
That sounded pretty cool.
I didn't do drugs or anything, but I was up for the challenge.
It said to meet at this bridge at this time, a Sunday afternoon or something, in the summertime in St.
Louis.
So I went there.
I didn't know that in St.
Louis there were about a dozen Buddhist groups of every stripe, and they regularly gathered.
What this gathering entailed was a couple of Dharma talks.
There must have been two or three hundred people there.
When the Dharma talks ended, there's this old bridge that crosses the Mississippi River, called the Chain of Rocks Bridge.
It's so old that they can't use it for car traffic, and it has a bend about mid-span.
It's kind of weird for a bridge.
What we did was get our cushions, blankets, whatever we could carry, and walk along the bridge.
The bridge is about a [unclear: "crystal mile"] long.
We sat down on our blankets and cushions, and we meditated together.
I can still feel the breeze coming off the Mississippi, hitting me in the face, because it was, as usual, a pretty hot day.
And just the silence led me to my first Zen group.
I met some people there and they said, "Come on in, the water's fine."
So I did that.
I got together with some other people, and for a while, like he was talking about, they were my teachers.
I didn't want to jump in with both feet.
I just wanted to be there around the periphery and find out a little bit of what they knew.
After I had been there for a while, I met the teacher there.
He was Japanese, classically trained.
He spent his time between Tokyo and St.
Louis.
He had to be housed in both locations, so when he wasn't teaching university, he came back to St.
Louis.
I remember meeting him for the first time.
I walked up to this old two-story cottage-type house, from the turn of the last century.
And there's this old Japanese dude in this great big front yard, [unclear: "They lost around that old park tower a couple acres"].
So figure about an acre of front lawn with trees hanging over it.
He's kneeling on the lawn, picking something.
I thought he was picking crabgrass, but what he was picking was blades of grass.
It was shady enough that moss would grow in the front yard along with the grass.
He wanted his front yard to be all moss, like it was in some of the temples in Japan.
I kneeled down next to him and started watching him, and started picking the grass.
He didn't say a word to me.
He was picking the grass for about half an hour.
Then he got up, went inside, and we started the meditation.
But as it turned out, he was [unclear: "the avid"].
And I picked a lot more grass after that, I might add.
I was back there a couple of years ago, and it looks like he's just about there.
I don't know if you've ever seen some of the Japanese gardens, where it's nothing but moss.
It looks like green velvet.
It's absolutely gorgeous.
So I got a teacher, and it was really a great experience.
The question is, is it okay to have several teachers, to have changed teachers?
And I'm like Edie.
I didn't roam around in some of the lofty teaching situations that you did.
I was in the Midwest.
Not so many Zen teachers in the Midwest.
You've got to really dig.
But I really think it's essential.
He said we change teachers when outside forces make us do so.
He also stresses the need for a long-term commitment to a single teacher if at all possible.
The personal relationship between student and teacher makes it possible for the teacher to steer the student to those areas of Zen that make it possible for him to grow with the Dharma.
And I agree.
But there's always a button, it seems like, with Zen.
I think it's important to sit and learn from all kinds of teachers.
Zen is an absolutely huge and complex subject, at least I found it so.
And I think that every teacher you meet knows one little area of Zen that maybe nobody else knows.
It's almost like, if you've ever been lucky enough to go inside an old European or Gothic cathedral, and you look at those beautiful stained glass windows.

I really think that if you only have one teacher and don't work with other people or listen to other people, it's like looking at one shard of glass in the stained glass window, red for example, and thinking the whole window is red when it's not.
You can only get a feeling of the beauty and magnificence of the window by looking at as much of it as you possibly can, and standing back.
In the short term, Norm says it's broadening and interesting.
Well, that's true.
But like I said, I think it's a lot more than that.
I think it is important in one way: if you do nothing but listen to many teachers, it's really easy to get confused, listening to all these different points of view.
It's a little like flip-flopping channels between MSNBC and Fox all day long.
You get pretty confused, as I would.
So I think the long-term teacher who knows us well can keep us on our track.
He or she is our touchstone, if you will, and keeps us grounded.
I may have learned something really neat over here, but I can go back to the touchstone and see how valuable the information was.
So I think, yeah, you have to have both.
I have talked to you about my first teacher, [unclear: "who was on Yeshida"].
Dokusan with him was really a challenge, to say the least.
His favorite saying was, "Well, just sit," and that would solve everything.
"Just sit some more."
And he sat and sat and sat.
I remember going to my first dokusan with him.
I had this problem at work with another coworker, and the situation was this and that and the other thing.
He listened to that, and after I finished my sob story, he said, "Well, just don't do that."
I hadn't considered that.
And he was so gentle.
He wouldn't give a long Dharma talk, but as we were sitting, in a real small room, [unclear: "Grace went through it"].
Every once in a while he would come up with almost a haiku, just something for you to kick around in your mind while you were sitting.
So it was a very, very gentle form of instruction, other than dokusan.
My second teacher was Kaylin McAllister, and I know nobody's ever heard of her.
She's an absolute phenomenon.
If you want to talk about bodhisattvas and what a bodhisattva is, all you have to do is look and see what she's done.
It's amazing.
I was lucky enough to meet her at my first group.
What we were doing at the time was that she was really into prison work, going to some of the prisons in Missouri and spending a couple of hours meditating and talking with the inmates.
What was really neat about that was that it was a two-and-a-half-hour drive one way from St.
Louis to the prison.
So it was a captive two-and-a-half-hour training session.
And then back the same thing, with the meditation and maybe a Mexican meal on the side.
Good Mexican food.
But she was always doing that.
She was working as a landscape contractor, putting in some fantastic hours, and she was barely making the mortgage payments every month on her house.
Yet if somebody needed something, she was right there, to the point where I would be on her: "Hey, you really need to have a little bit of extra money so you can pay for your health insurance.
That would be good."
So I was griping at her quite a bit, and she kept trucking.
She felt the need to, you know, when somebody gets out of prison, they have nothing.
I think the state of Missouri kicks them out the door.
They have their prison greys, and they have twenty bucks, and they have a bus ticket.
And they're supposed to find a job, find an apartment, be a contributing member of society.
It didn't work very well.
So her big push was finding some type of job for these convicts to do.
She liked to cook pastries, brownies, cookies, chocolate pies.
So she said, "We'll do that."
I said, "You're nuts.
You're crazy.
Where are you going to do that?"
"Well, we'll start in my kitchen, but we'll buy a bakery."
Okay.
Go online and look at Laughing Bear Bakery in St.
Louis.
She did it.
They have a full-fledged bakery there, [unclear: "This man by inmates"], and it comes up with all these pastries.
Not only that, she dabbles in helping homeless people as well.
I don't think there's five minutes of her day she's not doing something for somebody else, or trying to make a living so she can help somebody else.
That's her whole life.
She has my vote.
I can't imagine somebody putting in any more effort than she does.
And she had a great sense of humor.
She has a great sense of humor.
Loves practical jokes.
Loves going through second-hand stores.
Loves making snow angels out in the snow in front of the [unclear: "models"].
Loves making snow angels out in the snow in front of the monastery when it's twenty degrees.
Loves all those things.
They say that we change teachers as circumstances and our needs change.
Well, she introduced me to my third teacher, [unclear: "Shogun Weinkauf"], and he runs a monastery in Iowa, [unclear: "the Koura of Iowa, Kouramanshi"] Dragon's Gate.
The monastery was built from plans that came from Japan, of a contemporary Buddhist monastery.
He's finished all the buildings now, and it's going great.
I wanted to learn more, so I stepped into his world.
Like I said, it was a monastery, and most of the people there were priests of all the little Buddhist groups around the Minneapolis, Midwest, St.
Louis area.
And can you imagine trying to run a Buddhist monastery in rural Iowa, where the only thing you've got is cows moving in the background, and getting along with everybody?
But he could.
You talk about leading a group, how to talk to conservative people: he's got a [unclear: "wire"].
He does it all the time, and they respond to it as well.
So I got a lot of my acceptance from him.
And his teaching style was a little bit different.
His big thing was, do what you need to do right now, right now, whether you want to or not.
I would go and he would say something and I would kick it around.
And if I had a problem, I'd go to him in dokusan and say, "I've got this problem."
Most of the time he wouldn't give me a direct answer.
He'd say, "Well, think on that a little bit more."
He was always pushing me, not telling me what to do, but pushing me toward a better answer than the one I had.
I think that really is a large part of Zen for me today.
He kept saying, "Well, you've got the right answers.
You just need to keep thinking on it a little bit longer."
And maybe that's our final teacher: ourself.
And Norm says in here that at some point the student, if he perseveres, can pass the teacher to another teacher.
Five minutes.
Wow.
That was such a sign.
Because after this it got depressing.
So we could end on a high note.
And I think that might be the goal of the whole exercise.
When we can be comfortable in our own skin, and when we're not upset with life in general, we're well on the way.
And now I'm at Red Cedar with you guys.
Is that the depressing part?
I paid him ten bucks to say that.
No.
I just wanted you to know that this is such a great group, and I learn from each one of you that I come in contact with every time I show up here.
It's a real joy.
It is a real joy.
You are an A-class bunch of people.
I am really grateful for the opportunity.
There are so many opportunities to study here, to formally study.
And I encourage you, if you're not signing up for a course, do it, because you'll never find better instruction.
I'm finding my place here, as Norman's saying.
And I think I might have talked about that.
And I would talk about Tim, and it's great that he's not here, because it makes you see the profession.
It's going really good, and then there's Tim.
He's recording.
It's going on the boat.
But Tim, we're developing a pretty good relationship, and I'm really enjoying myself.
And Tim, I would say what I really thought of him, but it might give him a big head, and he might be asking for a bigger stipend the next time negotiations roll around.
But we've got a good teacher, and we've got some great teachers, the opportunities for some great teachers to come through here.
So really, you've got your long-term teacher, and you can see these little bits and pieces of shards of glass that come floating through here from time to time.
And it just doesn't get any better than that.
Thank you.
*May our intention deeply extend to our green place where...*

verbatim.text: A Dharma seminar for July, which is about the book, What is Zen, that Norman Fischer and Susan Moon wrote and published together, What is Zen. So this evening's topic is teachers. And I'm going to start, and then Scott is going to finish. So that's done. Okay, thank you. There are questions in this book, and then Susan asked the questions and some of them are elaborate questions and some of them are simple and then Norman answers in really clear clarifying way I highly recommend the book, whether you're new or old or long term or short term. It's a lovely book. So I'm going to answer some of the early questions in that chapter. The first one is do you have to have a teacher.

And Norman says no, you don't. Zazen is a practice in and of itself that anyone can do. And it's a practice on its own right, you learn a lot from doing it. However, if you can find a teacher and work with a teacher, you will be you will benefit greatly. I will help you interpret your experience, it will help you learn Buddhist teachings and Zen teachings, and you will grow as a person. The Sangha and the teachers are really integral and interrelated and in a way you can't have really full Zen experience without teachers, including all of us. So members as well as designated teachers. I'm going to tell you a little bit about my first teachers. My first one was straight out of Japan. Back in the 70s.

He was invited by Suzuki Roshi who was the head of the San Francisco Sand Center and starting in the late 60s. And he invited Koban who lived in Japan and was part of a temple family. He invited him to come over and help set up Tassajara which the San Francisco Sand Center had recently purchased and set it up as a monastery. The first Japanese monastery in the U.S. And I guess the only one on the west coast still. And Koban then became a teacher at Haikusendo which was in Los Altos, California, which is about 40 miles south of San Francisco. Suzuki Roshi had a student who lived in Los Altos who invited him to come down to Suzuki Roshi to come down maybe every week or every two weeks or so to give a talk there. And he gathered some students there.

And so when Koban moved there, he moved into that neighborhood, he and his family, and he became the teacher for the Haikusendo group which was flourishing at that point. So I met Koban probably two years after he was first in the U.S. and became that teacher. I had been reading about Zen and found it perplexing and fascinating. And I began to sense Zen based on that book, The Three Pillars of Zen, which had illustrations in the back about how you sit down, which is just totally bizarre. It's like trying to learn yoga through illustrations. And I did it for a while and I thought I'm sure I'm not doing this right and I wish I could talk with somebody about it. And just then, like the next week, in the newspaper there was an ad saying that this teacher, Japanese teacher, was going to come to Foothill College and teach a class for a full quarter on Zen. So I thought this is my chance.

And I signed up and I was really scared to go because I thought it was very unusual. It was not at all what my background had been, but I was really wanting to learn about it. So I expected there might be 10 or 12 students there. When I got there, there were like 80 students in this room and there were nearly enough chairs and a lot of us were sitting on the floor and we waited and waited and waited for about 20 minutes after the class started. And finally he, Kobun, who was maybe in mid-30s at that time, he kind of floated in with this beautiful black gown and precise collar, very unlike mine, and bald shiny head and big smile on his face. And he was just like some kind of visitation, you know, it was just really wonderful. And he spoke English pretty well but he had a very thick Japanese accent. So you didn't get, I didn't get much of what he said, but he was just so inspiring in his being that he seemed like a wonderful, wonderful person.

And toward the end of this 10-week course, he invited some of us, anybody who wanted to, to come to the Haiku Zendo on Wednesday evenings like they had Wednesday evenings in those days too, like we do now. And so a few of us went and the zendo was in a two-car garage in the home of this woman who had initially invited Suzuki Roshi to talk there. And they had converted it into a beautiful zendo. And it was just like spectacular, so exotic and full of incense and candlelight and beautiful zabutans and zafus and tatami mats and all that. It was just like, I don't know, a dream. And I was just immediately captivated by the whole thing and never, never, ever missed a single night ever after that and joined the group, the sangha. I became a regular student, went to classes, went to a lot of things there and tried to understand what zin was about. And there was a thing that you could have dokusan with the teacher and I didn't know what that was about or what you were supposed to say.

And so I had been a pretty academic person. So I took a lot of my books there and said, OK, now I want you to explain this and I want you to explain this and that kind of stuff. That was the way he was very patient with me. I kept asking about what's this emptiness? What does that mean? And he would say he would say something that I didn't understand, of course. And so I would ask him again and again. And finally, he gave me this book of Narachuna. It's the third century scholar on Buddhism explaining emptiness and was called emptiness.

And of course, it was totally indecipherable for me. And I thought, well, that was really a joke. That was his answer. You can't explain emptiness. Or if you could explain it, nobody could understand what it was. So Cobin was a lovely, lovely person. We have a picture here in our ancestors thing in the library. This is Cobin as a bit older person than he was when he first arrived.

You might look at that. There's a wonderful book put out by one of his students in more recent years that gives lots of pictures of him and lots of sayings of his. He was particularly kind and receptive to people and just said, you know, you're fine just as you are. And I really appreciated that because in those days, I wasn't feeling that I was at all fine. Let's read something that's like that. He said, listen to the truth. If there's any misunderstandings about what is called Zen life or Buddhist life, I'd like to clear them up and reassure you that however you are is the way you should be.

Sweet. And Buddha's enlightenment and humankind has a topic. When we are in the muddy road, to hate being in the muddy road doesn't do anything. The first thing is to step out of it or to find how to walk in the muddy road. Hatred is extra. If there is some problem, kindly deal with it and take care of it yourself in the right way. So he was able to work with students where the student was. And so even though I didn't know quite how to handle going to him for dokusan later, a few years later, as still he was still my teacher.

And I had a big crisis in my family. My husband was going to die. And I knew that. And I called Cobin and said, what should I do? And Cobin helped me with that very directly in a very practical way. And when my husband did die, he was a suicide. And Cobin was right there, came immediately to my house and did a ceremony for me and did other following ceremonies. He just was a person who just accepted where everyone was and supported us wherever we needed that support.

So he was a wonderful teacher. Until about five years into my being part of Haikusendō and his student, I did ask for jukai and was given a rakusu and took the precepts and so forth. But sometime after that, he decided that he didn't want to teach there anymore. He didn't want to be the head of a sangha. He wanted to be a traveling teacher and had all over the world places to go and teach and so forth. Well, everyone was shocked. I didn't know what to think of that. And I myself, I thought you had to have a teacher for life.

You know, that was it. You got only one chance and then they couldn't go away. It was kind of the Guro time where you followed forever. And it turns out that Zen doesn't require that, fortunately. But some people wouldn't let him go. They just moved with him to where he went. You know, to New Mexico, Santa Cruz, California, wherever it was, they went with him and I suppose supported him in some way. But I thought he had been so helpful to me and he truly wanted to escape from us, to not do that type of leadership anymore.

So I, with a lot of pain, gave him up, you know, gave him away, allowed him to leave us, and didn't see him more than a couple of times after that, every long time. He was always very warmly happy to see me when that happened. So it was a true love relationship with this teacher. It was wonderful to have that early in my Zen life. So I was without that kind of contact and connection for a good ten years. And then I met and began to sit with Reb Anderson. I do also have a picture of him at San Francisco Zen Center.

He was and has been an avid at the San Francisco Zen Center. And a very fine teacher, very bright, brilliant guy, very analytical, very unconventionally, not so social. Maybe didn't know all of it, but very refined and so forth. He was an amazing teacher for me because during the years that I was studying with Kobe and couldn't understand some of the things that he said, I missed a lot of teachings, I think. And Reb had a lot of insight into the Buddhist teachings about emptiness, for one thing. No self, how perception happens, karma, things like that, that are really abstruse and difficult for Westerners to understand.

So I learned a great deal from him. And I went, the final thing that I did with him was in 2000, I went to a winter three-week practice period at Green Gulch Monastery. That's part of the San Francisco group. And I had forgotten to take my rakusu from the coven had given me many years before. And I thought, oh, this is, I was really crushed that I had forgotten. This thing is so precious to me. And then I finally thought, well, maybe it's time for me to let him go entirely. It was maybe 20 years or something since he'd been, I'd been close with him.

So I talked to Reb about it and I asked him, would he be willing to give me the precepts again? And I'd already arranged for him to be my teacher and he had accepted that. So he did do that. And so I made my first raka suit. The coven had given me one from Japan, but I made one for myself. And that was a lovely experience. And then Reb was my teacher for the next probably about six years, seven years, something like that. And I got a lot from him going.

He not only taught at Green Gulch, but he was no longer Abbott. So he could teach more widely and he did retreats at various other centers. And I was able to practice with him and learn so much from him. Then I came here, 15, going on 16 years ago, moved up here. And Tim joined the practice group that we were developing and took over time. And Tim was the main guy, the head guy then and grew and grew and became, you know, not only ordained, but transmitted as a teacher and became now, now he's our, what do we call him? A guiding teacher and so forth.

And he was kind enough to ordain me as a priest five years ago in 2013. So the second question that I wanted to answer from the book was, can you have more than one teacher? Well, yeah, I did. I found out that I could and I was really happy that I had those opportunities. And I lived in an area in California until 2003 when I came here, which was just loaded with all kinds of Buddhist teachers. So I had lots of opportunities to study with many different teachers. Jack Kornfield, you've probably heard of.

I studied with him quite a bit. And with Norman when he was at Green Gulch as a priest, with somebody called Gil Kronzdale who's written a number of things. And he's both a Zen teacher and a Vipassana teacher. Yvonne Rand who was his old Zen teacher from the original group of people, who then learned a lot of Tibetan practices. And I studied with her for a certain amount of time. I was able to go and sit with Thich Nhat Hanh at two different large group meetings and hear him speak.

I joined and practiced with various Tibetan groups and Vipassana groups. So it was kind of a smorgasbord that was going on in the Bay Area and everything. So it's good to experience numerous other teachers. And we actually have a fair number of really good teachers within our reach. We have Kate and Michael up in British Columbia who are fine teachers. And have Sunday, I think they're open practices on Sundays, and you could go up there. Seattle Soto Zen, we can go down and visit with them and sit with them also I think on Sundays. The Olympia Zen Center has a lovely zendo and a regular practice that we can take part in.

Anita Feng is a Korean Zen practice in the northern part of Seattle. The VIMS group here that we share the building with has frequently good teachers coming for weekends or even for just one evening's talk and we can take advantage of that. And of course we can, and people have done, gone to other zendo centers in Oregon and in California. So if you want to, you can do it. But also teachers, our sangha members, just us, us who bump around against each other, like getting a rock polisher, that's the metaphor for what the sangha life is. It wears down our sharp edges and polishes us up, and sometimes it's uncomfortable,

but we live through it and we're grateful for it. So sangha members are also our regular teachers daily and we practice silently together, which teaches us a lot. And we work as volunteers together, which teaches us even more, because sometimes we don't work in the same ways and struggle together. And we benefit from the wisdom and talent of each other as Dharma friends. So we're not social friends. My experience with sangha members is that we're not social friends,

so much as we're essential spiritual friends, and that's a very special relationship. We also here have a mentoring program where newer people can request mentoring, which is meeting with a more senior person for a period of time of six months or a year periodically and talk about what the student wants. We have lots of Dharma talks and dokusan and practice discussions and shuso classes when we have a shuso head student. So we do have lots of ways of teaching each other. Third and last, what is meant by zen training?

Sometimes you hear I'm training as a zen student. And training is what, in a way, it's kind of boot camp. If you're in a sesshin, it feels like it's a big rigorous effort. But zazen is training the mind and body, watching the mind carefully, observing what it's doing, and training the body to move in specific, very finely tuned ways, working with the breath, working with posture, working with movement. Buddhist teachings train us how to conceive and think about reality from a certain perspective. A teacher can be like a coach or a music teacher.

You're both devoted to the practice, and the teacher guides you, the student, toward better and better expression. Learning all the zen's forms is a kind of training. How to hold the hands, how to sit correctly, how to sit quietly, how to move in the zendo, how to bow, how to work with the altar, all the different roles, very specific things that you learn. And so those are trainings. Zazen and the forms instill discipline.

They want us to be exact here, now, paying attention. Reb once said that he could tell when people are trying too hard by looking how they move in the zendo. They're kind of exaggerating their erectness or something, or if they're not quite sure they really should be doing this, they're kind of doubtful and maybe resist and they kind of slide in here and do that. So he said a lot can be seen in the physical behavior of people, as to where they are, and he encouraged everyone to be just right there,

doing it enough, but not too much, that kind of thing. That's being in the present, which is the big teaching. That's what I want to say. Can you keep time for me? Okay. Maybe. Well, that one makes too much noise. Okay, you have a good half hour.

The first question I wanted to address was, do you have to have a teacher in order to practice zen? And Norm says, it depends on what your intentions, goals, and circumstances are. And I'm lucky enough to talk with a lot of newcomers. And they're, you know, when I ask them, why are you here? And usually about nine times out of ten, they'll say something like, well, I read a couple of books on the subject. It sounds interesting.

And I've meditated a couple of times. I'm a very recent graduate. And that was my story too. In my travels through Asia, I saw thousands and thousands of people that didn't have too much material wealth. They were living in little shacks along the river generally. But they seemed so happy. And you go about every block, there's another Buddhist temple or shrine.

And I said, well, maybe there's something to this Buddhism thing. So I did the same thing, read a few books, started meditating. Didn't even think about a teacher. It wasn't even in my brain scan at that point. Which seems kind of primitive now, but I remember reading a story about John Day of Laura. He's a recently deceased abbot of the Mountain and Rivers Order in New York. And he started out the same way.

He read a few books. And he meditated. He was working at a job. The only quiet place he could find was a closet. So he would meditate during his lunch break sitting in a closet. And then it grew from there. I fully believe that that old saying, when you're ready, a teacher will appear.

And it did for me. I got the feeling that I needed to practice with other people. I was thinking more in terms of a car club or something like that. I wasn't thinking about a Zen center. But I knew I just wanted to be with other people that shared my interests. And not too long thereafter, I was lucky enough to see an ad in the newspaper.

And the ad said, change your mind today. That sounded pretty cool. I didn't do drugs or anything, but I was up for the challenge. And it said, well, meet at this bridge at this time. And it said it was like a Sunday afternoon or something. In the summertime in St. Louis.

And so I went there. And I didn't know that in St. Louis, there was about a dozen Buddhist groups of every stripe. And they regularly gathered. And what this gathering entailed was, we had a couple of Dharma talks. And there must have been two or three hundred people there. And so when the Dharma talks ended,

there's this old bridge that crosses the Mississippi River. It's called the Chain of Rocks Bridge. And it's so old that they can't use it for car traffic. And it has a bend about mid-span. It's kind of weird, like a bridge. And what we did was we got our cushions, blankets, whatever we could carry. And we walked along the bridge.

And the bridge is about a crystal mile long. And we sat down on our blankets and cushions. And we meditated together. I could still feel the feeling of the breeze coming off the Mississippi, getting me in the face, because it was, as usual, a pretty hot day. And just the silence that led me to my first Zen group. I met some people there and they said,

come on in, the water's fine. So I did that. So I got with some other people. And for a while, like he was talking about, they were my teachers. I didn't want to jump in with both feet. I just wanted to kind of be there around the periphery and find out a little bit of what they knew. After I had been there for a while,

the teacher there was a Japanese, classically trained. He spent his time between Tokyo and St. Louis. He had to be housed in both locations. So when he wasn't teaching university, he came back to St. Louis. So I can remember, I remember meeting him for the first time. And I walked up to this old, it was a turn of the last century, cottage type house, two story house. And there's this old Japanese dude in this great big front yard.

They lost around that old park tower a couple acres. So figure about an acre front lawn with trees hanging over it. And there's this old Japanese guy. He's kneeling on the lawn, and he's picking something. Well, I thought he was picking crab grass. But what he was picking was blades of grass. You see, it was dark enough to where moss would grow in the front yard along with the grass.

And he wanted his front yard to be all moss, like it was in some of the temples in Japan. And I kneeled down next to him and started watching him. Started picking the grass. He didn't say a word to me. He was picking the grass in there for about a half an hour. And then he got up, went inside, and we started the meditation. But as it turned out, he was the avid.

And I picked a lot more grass after that too, I might add. And I was back there a couple years ago, and it looks like he's just about there. I don't know if you've ever seen some of the Japanese gardens, and it's nothing but moss. You know, it looks like green velvet. It's absolutely gorgeous. So I got a teacher, and it was really a great experience.

The question is, is it okay to have several teachers that have changed teachers? And I'm like Edie. I didn't roam around in some of the lofty teaching situations that you did. I was in the Midwest. Not so many Zen teachers in the Midwest. You got to really dig.

But I think it's, I really think it's essential. He said we change teachers when outside forces make us do so. He also stresses the need for a long-term commitment to a single teacher if at all possible. And the personal relationship between student and teacher makes it possible for the teacher to steer the student to those areas of Zen that make it possible for him to grow with the Dharma.

And I agree. But, and there's always a button, Zen, it seems like. I think it's important to sit and learn from all kinds of teachers. Zen is an absolutely huge and complex subject. At least I found it so. And I think that every teacher that you meet knows one little area of Zen

that maybe nobody else knows. It's almost like looking, if you've ever been lucky enough to go inside an old European or a Gothic cathedral and you look at those beautiful stained glass windows. And I really think that if you only have one teacher and don't work with other people or listen to other people, it's like looking at one shard of glass in the stained glass window, red for example,

and thinking the whole window is red when it's not. You can only get a feeling of the beauty and magnificence of a little window by looking as much of it as you possibly can and standing back. You know, in the short term, Norm says it's broadening and interesting. Well, that's true. But like I said, I think it's a lot more than that.

I think it is important in one way. If you do nothing but listen to many teachers, it's really easy to get confused, listening to all these different points of view. It's a little like maybe flip-flopping channels between MSNBC and Fox all day long. You get pretty confused, as I would. So I think that the long-term teacher that knows us well

can keep us kind of on our track. He or she is our touchstone, if you will, keeps us grounded. You know, I may have learned something really neat over here, but I can go back to the touchstone and see how valuable the information was. So I think really, yeah, you have to have both. I have talked to you about my first teacher,

who was on Yeshida. And he was really... Tokusan with him was really a challenge, to say the least. His favorite saying was, well, just sit, and that would solve everything. Just sit some more. And he sat and sat and sat.

And I remember going to my first tokusan with him, and I had this problem at work, you know, with this other coworker, and the situation was this and that and the other thing. And he goes on and listened to that. And after I finished my sod story, he said, well, just don't do that. I hadn't considered that.

And he was so gentle. He wouldn't give a long Dharma talk, but as we were sitting, and it was a real small room, we were sitting and Grace went through it. And every once in a while, he would come up with almost a haiku, just something for you to kick around in your mind

while you were sitting. So it was a real, a very, very gentle form of instruction, other than tokusan. My second teacher was Kaylin McAllister, and I know nobody's ever heard of her. She's an absolute phenomenon. If you want to talk about bodhisattvas and what a bodhisattva is,

all you have to do is look and see what she's done. You know, it's amazing. I was lucky enough to meet her at my first group, and I went with her to, actually what we were doing at the time was she was really into prison work, going to some of the prisons in Missouri and spending a couple hours meditating

and talking with the inmates. And so what was really neat about that was that it was a two and a half hour drive one way to get to the prison from St. Louis. So it was kind of a captive two and a half hour training session. And then back the same thing with the meditation and maybe a Mexican meal on the side. Good Mexican food.

But she was always doing that. And she was working as a landscape contractor, putting in some fantastic hours. And she was barely making the mortgage payments every month on her house. But yet, if somebody needed something, she was right there to the point where I would be on her. Hey, you really need to have a little bit of extra money

so you can pay for your health insurance. That would be good. So I was griping at her quite a bit, and she kept trucking. And she felt the need to, you know, when somebody gets out of prison, they have nothing. I think the state of Missouri kicks them out the door,

they have their prison grades, and they have 20 bucks, and they have a bus ticket. And they're supposed to find a job, find an apartment, you know, be a contributing member of society. It didn't work very well. And so her big push was finding some type of job

for these convicts to do. Well, she liked to cook pastries, brownies, cookies, chocolate pies. So she said, we'll do that. I said, you're nuts. You're crazy. Where are you going to do that? Well, we'll start in my kitchen,

but we'll get, we'll buy a bakery. Okay. And go online and look at Laughing Bear Bakery in St. Louis. She did it. They have a full-fledged bakery there. This man by inmates, you know, comes up with all these pastries.

Not only that, she dabbles in helping homeless people as well. I don't think there's five minutes of her day she's not doing something for somebody else or trying to make a living so she can help somebody else. That's her whole life. I think that's a strong, you know,

she has my vote. I can't imagine somebody putting in any more effort at the time than she does. And she had a great sense of humor. She has a great sense of humor. Loves practical jokes. Loves going through second-hand stores. Loves making snow angels out in the snow

in front of the models. Loves making snow angels out in the snow in front of the monastery when it's 20 degrees. Loves all those things. She introduced me, you know, they say that we change teachers as their circumstances and our needs change. Well, she introduced me to my third teacher,

Shogun Weinkauf, and he runs a monastery of the Koura of Iowa, Kouramanshi Dragon's Gate. And the monastery was built from plans that came from Japan of a contemporary Buddhist monastery. And he's finished all the buildings now

and it's going great. So I wanted to learn more. And so I stepped into his world. And like I said, it was a monastery and most of the people there were priests of all the little Buddhist groups around, you know, the Minneapolis Midwest, St. Louis area.

And he found it, you know, can you imagine trying to run a Buddhist monastery in rural Iowa where the only thing you've got are cows moving in the background and getting along with everybody. But he could.

You know, you talk about, you know, you're leading a group how to talk to conservative people. He's got a wire. He does it all the time. And they respond to it as well. So I got a lot of my acceptance from him. And his teaching style was a little bit different.

His big thing was, do what you need to do right now, right now. Whether you want to or not. And so I would go and he would say something and I would kick it around. And if I had a problem, I'd go to him in Dokushan and say,

I've got this problem. And most of the time he wouldn't give me a direct answer. He'd say, well, think on that a little bit more. He was always pushing me, not telling me what to do, but pushing me toward a better answer than the one I had.

And I think that really is a large part of Zen for me today. You know, he kept saying, well, you've got the right answers. You just need to keep thinking on it a little bit longer. And maybe that's our final teacher, is ourself. And Norm says in here that
at some point the student, if he perseveres, can pass the teacher to another teacher. Five minutes. Wow. That was such a sign. Because after this it got depressing.

So we could end on a high note. And I think that might be the goal of the whole exercise. When we can be comfortable in our own skin, and when we're not upset with life in general, you know, we're well on the way.
And now I'm at Red Cedar with you guys. Is that the depressing part? I paid him ten bucks to say that. No. I just wanted you to know that this is such a great group, and I learn from each one of you

that I come in contact with every time I show up here. It's a real joy. It is a real joy. You are an A-class bunch of people. I am really grateful for the opportunity. There are so many opportunities to study here,
to formally study. And I encourage you, if you're not signing up for a course, do it, because you'll never find better instruction. I'm finding my place here, as Norman's saying.

And I think I might have talked about that And I would talk about Tim, and it's great that he's not here, because it makes you see the profession. You know, it's going really good, and then there's Tim. He's recording. It's going on the boat.

But, you know, Tim, we're developing a pretty good relationship, and I'm really enjoying myself. And Tim, I would say what I really thought of him, but it might give him a big head, and he might be asking for

a bigger stipend the next time, you know, negotiations roll around. But we've got a good teacher, and we've got some great teachers, the opportunities for some great teachers to come through here. So really, you know, you've got your long-term teacher,

and you can see these little bits and pieces of shards of glass that come floating through here from time to time. And it just doesn't get any better than that. Thank you. May our intention deeply extend
to our green place where...
